clinicalPearls: A benign renal tumour composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle and mature fat, part of the PEComa family
Most are sporadic, solitary and found incidentally; multiple bilateral lesions suggest tuberous sclerosis complex
The presence of macroscopic fat on CT or MRI is characteristic and usually allows a confident diagnosis
Fat-poor variants can mimic renal cell carcinoma and may require biopsy or excision to clarify
Larger lesions carry a risk of spontaneous, potentially life-threatening retroperitoneal haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome)
Aneurysms within the feeding vessels increase the bleeding risk and can be targeted by embolisation
Epithelioid angiomyolipoma is an uncommon variant with malignant potential
reference.pathophysiology: Angiomyolipomas are benign mesenchymal neoplasms arising from perivascular epithelioid cells and containing a variable mixture of dysmorphic thick-walled vessels, smooth muscle and adipose tissue. In tuberous sclerosis, biallelic inactivation of the TSC1 or TSC2 genes leads to constitutive activation of the mTOR pathway, driving multiple and often larger tumours. The abnormal, aneurysm-prone vasculature accounts for the tendency of larger lesions to bleed. The epithelioid variant shows atypical cells and can behave in a malignant fashion.
additionalDifferentials: Fat-poor angiomyolipoma versus renal cell carcinoma
Clear cell or papillary renal cell carcinoma
Renal lipoma or other fatty lesion
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI to demonstrate macroscopic fat and characterise the lesion
Assessment of lesion size and intratumoural aneurysms to gauge bleeding risk
Screening for tuberous sclerosis features when lesions are multiple or bilateral
Renal mass biopsy when imaging is indeterminate and malignancy cannot be excluded
Baseline renal function, particularly before intervention
redFlags: Acute flank pain with hypotension suggesting spontaneous haemorrhage
Rapidly enlarging lesion or a large lesion with prominent aneurysms
Features suggesting the epithelioid variant or malignancy
New multiple bilateral lesions raising concern for a syndrome with other organ involvement
reference.prognosis: Most angiomyolipomas are benign with an excellent prognosis; the main risks are haemorrhage from larger lesions and, rarely, malignant behaviour of the epithelioid variant, both of which can be mitigated by surveillance and timely intervention.
pitfalls: Assuming all angiomyolipomas are benign and overlooking the epithelioid variant
Misdiagnosing a fat-poor lesion as, or overlooking, renal cell carcinoma
Failing to evaluate for tuberous sclerosis when lesions are multiple
Underestimating haemorrhage risk in large or aneurysmal lesions
references: WHO Classification of Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Manage small asymptomatic lesions with active imaging surveillance to track growth and bleeding risk
Offer an mTOR inhibitor such as everolimus or sirolimus to shrink tumours, particularly in tuberous-sclerosis-associated multiple or larger angiomyolipomas driven by mTOR activation
Perform selective arterial embolisation to reduce the bleeding risk of larger lesions and those containing intratumoural aneurysms, and as first-line control of acute haemorrhage
Reserve nephron-sparing surgery for large, symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain lesions and for fat-poor tumours that cannot be distinguished from renal cell carcinoma
Treat spontaneous retroperitoneal haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome) as an emergency with resuscitation and urgent embolisation or surgery
Screen for tuberous sclerosis complex when lesions are multiple or bilateral, and refer for genetic counselling and family assessment when the complex is confirmed
Monitor baseline renal function, especially before embolisation or surgery, to preserve nephron mass
